reference.source: Parsons' Diseases of the Eye / Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology
clinicalPearls: A sight- and life-threatening infection of the orbital tissues behind the orbital septum, most often spreading from adjacent (especially ethmoid) sinusitis
Key features distinguishing it from preseptal cellulitis are painful or restricted eye movements (ophthalmoplegia), proptosis, and pain on eye movement
Systemic signs of fever and malaise accompany a red, swollen, tender lid; a relative afferent pupillary defect signals optic nerve compromise
Reduced visual acuity, colour vision loss, or an afferent pupillary defect indicate optic nerve threat and demand emergency intervention
Commonest in children and frequently caused by Staphylococcus, Streptococcus, and Haemophilus species, sometimes anaerobes
Urgent contrast CT of the orbit and sinuses identifies subperiosteal or orbital abscess and sinus involvement
Requires admission and prompt intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics, with surgical drainage of abscesses or sinuses when needed
reference.pathophysiology: Orbital cellulitis is infection of the soft tissues posterior to the orbital septum. Infection most commonly extends directly from the paranasal sinuses (particularly the ethmoid, separated from the orbit only by the thin lamina papyracea), but can also arise from trauma, dacryocystitis, dental infection, or haematogenous spread. Inflammation and oedema within the confined bony orbit raise pressure, displace the globe forward (proptosis), impair extraocular muscle function, and can compress or ischaemically injure the optic nerve. Spread posteriorly risks cavernous sinus thrombosis, meningitis, and intracranial abscess.
additionalDifferentials: Orbital tumour or rhabdomyosarcoma in children
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced CT of the orbit, sinuses, and brain to detect abscess and sinus disease
Assessment of visual acuity, colour vision, pupil reactions, and eye movements
Swabs/cultures of any discharge or drained material
Ophthalmology and ENT review; consider MRI if intracranial extension is suspected
redFlags: Emergency — threatens vision (optic nerve compression) and life (cavernous sinus thrombosis, meningitis, intracranial abscess)
Reduced acuity, impaired colour vision, or a relative afferent pupillary defect indicate imminent optic nerve damage
Restricted or painful eye movements and proptosis distinguishing it from benign preseptal cellulitis
Bilateral involvement, drowsiness, or cranial nerve palsies suggesting cavernous sinus or intracranial spread
reference.prognosis: With prompt intravenous antibiotics and timely drainage the outlook is good, but delay can lead to permanent visual loss, intracranial complications, and death.
pitfalls: Mistaking sight-threatening orbital cellulitis for benign preseptal cellulitis and failing to assess eye movements and optic nerve function
Delaying CT imaging and abscess drainage
Treating as an outpatient rather than admitting for intravenous therapy
Overlooking the underlying sinusitis that needs concurrent treatment
management: Start prompt intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics covering staphylococci (including MRSA), streptococci, Haemophilus and anaerobes
Arrange surgical drainage of subperiosteal or orbital abscess and sinus drainage (functional endoscopic sinus surgery) for abscess or failure to improve on antibiotics
Obtain urgent contrast CT of orbit, sinuses and brain with combined ophthalmology and ENT assessment
Monitor visual acuity, colour vision and pupillary reactions serially, with emergency intervention including orbital decompression if the optic nerve is threatened
Treat the underlying source, most often paranasal sinusitis, with nasal decongestants and supportive analgesia and antipyretics
Escalate to neurosurgery for intracranial extension, cavernous sinus thrombosis or brain abscess
